country: Gulf (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Iran risk)
summary: The US-Iran war that began Feb 28, 2026 has left the Strait of Hormuz mostly shut to commercial ships for over seven months. The war is now inside Saudi Arabia: Houthi strikes on Riyadh's airport killed at least 13 on Oct 10, and on Oct 14 a ballistic missile hit an Aramco office building at its Dhahran headquarters, damaging the floors used by top executives. Ships keep getting hit: UKMTO reported a tanker and two container ships struck near Hormuz on Oct 13. Brent was about $106.30 on the morning of Oct 14. A Houthi official said Russia and China have reached out about a ceasefire. Qatar shipped only 18 LNG cargoes in the war's first six months against 509 a year earlier. Most Gulf champions like Aramco are not US listed, so the US trade is through oil producers, US LNG exporters, oil service firms and the KSA ETF. On Oct 16 Brent settled at $109.86, its highest since May 19, after a record pace of ship attacks near Hormuz, and on Oct 17 a missile aimed at Yanbu, the Saudi port that bypasses Hormuz, was shot down. On Oct 17 Iran said its seven day plan to reopen Hormuz still stands if the US lifts its blockade and oil sanctions, and the Revolutionary Guards claimed a second supertanker hit a mine (not independently confirmed). On Oct 19 Brent touched $106.82 after the US waived new Russia tariffs, then settled at $109.55, down only 0.3%, and traded above $110 early Oct 20 after the Houthis claimed new strikes on Saudi sites at Yanbu and Shaybah (not confirmed by Saudi authorities). US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Gulf oil flows are back to about 80% of prewar levels, a US government figure, and that some sanctioned dark fleet tankers will be allowed to carry legal crude; Kpler thinks only about 24 qualify. On Oct 20 Iran's Revolutionary Guards said mines stopped three tankers near Hormuz; CENTCOM called the claims false and said the waterways are cleared of mines. Brent touched $111.99, then settled down 0.69% at $108.79 as Pakistan's army chief took a mediation plan to Tehran. Kpler counts at least 18 ships attacked in two weeks. On Oct 21 to 22 a drone strike on Aramco's Shaybah field killed two people without affecting operations, an attack on Dammam's airport killed one, and the US ordered some embassy staff to leave Saudi Arabia; Brent rose as much as 3.3% to $112.43.
for_you: This is the biggest outside risk to your whole dashboard. Oil above $100 because of Hormuz feeds US inflation, Fed hikes and market swings. Helped: CVX and LNG exporters. If you hold swings, a big Gulf headline is the most likely reason for a sudden gap down, so always have stops set.

changes.what: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the main route around Hormuz, was hit in several attacks. It restarted at a reduced rate by Sep 22, so Gulf oil exports stay limited.
Brent jumped about 4.8% to about $105 as Iran stepped up attacks on tankers in Hormuz.
Brent eased to about $104.7 after Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the November midterms. That lowers near term escalation risk but leaves the strait shut.

Houthi strikes on Riyadh's airport went on: Saturday's toll rose to at least 13 and a Sunday attack killed one more and wounded 11 (CNN). Iran called the latest US plan to reopen Hormuz 'insufficient', and Brent rebounded above $106 on Monday. Saudi stocks fell 0.15% Sunday and Qatar's index about 1.5%.
changes.for_you: If you hold swings, keep stops set: Gulf headlines are the most likely cause of a sudden gap. XOM and CVX are swing setups that need breakout volume, not just a headline. LNG gains while Qatar cargoes stay stuck.

changes.what: UKMTO reported a crude tanker hit by an unknown projectile while leaving Hormuz on Oct 11 and a product tanker hit on Oct 12, and the IRGC claimed more tanker strikes. Brent settled at $106.65 on Oct 12. Saudi stocks steadied, with the TASI up 0.33% on Oct 13.
changes.for_you: XOM is 0.4% from its 172.91 pivot but needs 20.4M+ shares on the breakout day; COP (new setup) needs 10M+ over 141.91. FRO is left out: tanker rates rise but so do the risks to its ships.

changes.what: A Houthi ballistic missile hit an Aramco administrative building at its Dhahran headquarters early Oct 14, causing a limited fire and damaging the top floors used by executives; reports differ on injuries (none per AP, four per Riyadh via IBTimes). On Oct 13 UKMTO reported a tanker struck in the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran said hit a mine, and two container ships hit by projectiles. Brent rose 0.58% to $106.30 and WTI 1.57% to $95.62 by 8:03am ET.
changes.for_you: Oil names stay helped, but a headline can cut both ways in one day. XOM is 0.4% from its 172.91 pivot and needs 20.4M+ shares to confirm; do not chase a gap. FRO is left out: rates rise but so does the risk to ships.

changes.what: A Houthi spokesman said Oct 14 that attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports will continue 'in the coming days' (House of Saud citing Reuters and gCaptain; less established source). Reuters reported the US is weighing letting sanctioned tankers carry non sanctioned oil out of the Gulf to cut record freight rates; analysts expect only a few extra ships. Brent fell about 1.5% to about $104.44 on Oct 15.
changes.for_you: COP closed over its 141.91 pivot on Oct 14, but the volume is not confirmed yet; wait for Setups. FRO is left out of both lists: more tankers allowed would ease freight rates, but the threats to shipping keep them high.

changes.what: Brent settled at $109.86 on Oct 16, up 3.7% and its highest since May 19, and WTI at $101.41, up 10.4% on the week. At least ten ships have been attacked in or near Hormuz since Oct 11, a record pace, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine. On Oct 17 the Saudi led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu, Saudi Arabia's Red Sea export port that bypasses Hormuz, and missiles hit Aden's airport on Oct 16. Iran denied a role in Houthi attacks and offered to mediate.
changes.for_you: Oil names stay helped and the energy swings on the scorecard are all in profit; keep the dashboard stops (XOM 162.99, CVX 210.45, COP 135.75) over the weekend because a ceasefire headline from Iran's mediation offer could gap oil down. OXY stays mixed: its Gulf assets sit in the war zone.

changes.what: On Oct 17 Iran's foreign minister said Tehran's seven day plan, sent through Qatar, still stands: the strait would reopen on day six if the US lifts its naval blockade and oil sanctions and agrees to a ceasefire that includes Lebanon (Tasnim). The US has rejected a return to the June terms. The same day the Revolutionary Guards claimed a second supertanker carrying over 2 million barrels hit a mine and stopped in the strait; there is no independent confirmation (Middle East Monitor).
changes.for_you: Oil faces two way risk at Monday's open: more mine claims push it up, a US reply to Iran's plan would push it down fast. If you hold energy swings, keep the dashboard stops (XOM 162.99, CVX 210.45, COP 135.75) and do not buy a gap up. FRO is left out of both lists: a reopening would ease freight rates, more attacks would raise them.

changes.what: The Russia waiver dip did not hold: Brent fell to $106.82 on Oct 19 but settled at $109.55, and traded above $110 early Oct 20 after Houthi claims of strikes on Yanbu and Shaybah (unconfirmed). Energy Secretary Wright said Gulf flows are back to about 80% of prewar levels and the US will let some sanctioned dark fleet tankers carry legal crude; Kpler estimates only about 24 ships qualify.
changes.for_you: If you hold energy swings, keep the dashboard stops; oil held up. Treat the 80% figure as a government claim until shipping data confirm it. LNG and FRO are left out of both lists: more legal tankers could ease freight rates, but Kpler expects little effect.

changes.what: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Oct 20 that mines stopped three tankers near Hormuz, two of them on fire; CENTCOM called the claims false and said the international waterways are cleared of mines, and no ship names have appeared. Brent touched $111.99 and settled at $108.79, down 0.69%, as Pakistan's army chief took a mediation plan to Tehran. United guided Q4 jet fuel at $4.80 a gallon against $3.90 in Q3.
changes.for_you: If you hold energy swings, keep the stops; oil is trading headlines with a $6 daily range. No airline buys or puts. FRO is left out of both lists: attacks raise tanker rates but also the risk to ships.

changes.what: A Houthi drone strike on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field killed two people but did not affect operations, a separate attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed one, and the US ordered some embassy staff and families to leave Saudi Arabia (Bloomberg, Oct 22). Brent settled at $108.82 on Oct 21 and rose as much as 3.3% to $112.43 early Oct 22. Trump denied the US is negotiating with Iran; Iran says indirect talks continue via Pakistan and Qatar.
changes.for_you: If you hold energy swings, keep the dashboard stops; XOM (178.09) and CVX (226.78) still have buyers leading on Oct 21. Do not add on a headline gap.
